place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 大比 · 第二轮 · 对卢方
place.en: Chending Temple · The contest · Round two · Against Lu Fang

setup.zh: 第二轮，对面是卢方：内门六层，金刃、土墙。他看了一眼石阶上的孙二狗，道：「外门的，一个比一个不知道天高地厚。」这一回，他没背手。
setup.en: Round two, and across from you is Lu Fang: layer six of the inner court, metal blade and earth wall. He glances at Sun Ergou on the steps: "Outer court — each one knows less of heaven and earth than the last." This time he doesn't put his hands behind his back.

recap.zh: 第二轮你对卢方：他的金刃、土墙，你火打给他看，木吃土；第三掌打裂了你的肋骨，你扒在台沿上，他踩着你的手碾——你从储物袋里摸出什么砸什么，碎的是那罐牛脂甘露；你看他的脚，等风，他一脚跺在牛油上，溜出台沿，你拿手腕勾了一下他的脚踝，内门的六层从你头顶上翻下了台。
recap.en: In round two you fought Lu Fang: against his metal blade and earth wall you threw fire for show and wood to eat the earth; his third palm cracked your rib, you hung from the rim and he ground your hand underfoot — you smashed down whatever your hand found in the pouch, and it was the jar of Beef-Tallow Nectar; you watched his feet, waited for the wind, his stamp came down on the tallow and skated off the rim, your wrist hooked his ankle, and the inner court's layer six went over your head and off the stage.

zh: 第二轮。对面，卢方，内门六层。
en: Round two. Across from you, Lu Fang, layer six of the inner court.
A metal blade, an earth wall.
Watch the wind first, then the deer.

story.zh:
那一上午，五行台上打了三轮。内门排头的祁长松，九层。秘境里他还是八层，守的是石坎：九层的师兄们下去挑灵草，他一个人守着那道坎，三天三夜，一个人也没放过去；那三天把他压实了，出来不到一个月，他破了九层。秘境十年一开，下一回，他等不起。这一颗丹，是他在内门站了二十年，头一回够得着的。内门里管他叫「祁不退」。他是土行的灵根，一掌推出来，掌上压着的是脚底下那一整块地；他不追，不绕，不跳，一招只进一步，一步一步，把对手压到台边，压下去，或是压得人自己认了输。二十年，没有人叫他往后退过一步。小满在台下看了他两场，看的不是他的脸，是他的脚：两场下来，那两只脚只往前走，没往后挪过一寸。

第二轮，小满对卢方。

卢方上台的时候，眼皮还是耷拉着，看了一眼小满，又看了一眼台下坐在石阶上的孙二狗，道：「外门的，一个比一个不知道天高地厚。」他没背手。这一回，他先出手了。

他右手一扬，一道白光从掌心里削出来，是金刃，贴着青石板削向小满的脚踝。小满往旁一跳，金刃削在台沿上，削下来一角石头。卢方吸了一口气——阿禾那张纸上写着的，一个字不差：使完金刃，要喘一口气——左手才往下一按，小满身前「轰」地拱起一堵土墙，齐胸高，把他往台边上挤。那一口气的工夫，小满两只手里早都攥好了。他右手一颗火弹打在土墙上，土墙只黑了一块；左手跟着一抖，一根木藤从土墙根底下钻了出去，土墙「咔」地裂了一道缝——火是打给卢方看的，木才是吃土的。台下有人「咦」了一声：「卢师兄换一样，还得喘一口气；他……他一口气扔了两样？」卢方的眼皮，头一回抬了起来。
story.en:
That morning three rounds were fought on the platform. Qi Changsong, first on the inner register, was layer nine. In the hidden realm he had still been eight, and what he held was the stone sill: the layer-nines went down to pick the herbs, and he alone held that sill three days and three nights and let no one past; those three days pressed him solid, and less than a month after coming out he broke through to nine. The hidden realm opens once in ten years; the next time, he couldn't wait. This pill was the first he had ever been within reach of, in twenty years standing in the inner court. In the inner court they called him Never-Back Qi. His root was earth, and when his palm went out, what rode on it was the whole piece of ground under his feet; he didn't chase, didn't circle, didn't leap — one step forward a move, step by step, he pressed his opponent to the edge and off it, or pressed him till he yielded. In twenty years no one had driven him back a single step. Xiaoman watched two of his bouts from below, and watched not his face but his feet: in two bouts those feet only went forward, and never moved an inch back.

Second round: Xiaoman against Lu Fang.

Lu Fang climbed up with his eyelids still drooping, glanced at Xiaoman, then at Sun Ergou sitting on the steps below. "Outer court — each one knows less of heaven and earth than the last." He didn't put his hands behind his back. This time he struck first.

His right hand flicked, and a white light sheared out of his palm — a metal blade, skimming the bluestone at Xiaoman's ankles. Xiaoman jumped aside; the blade sheared the stage's rim and took off a corner of stone. Lu Fang drew a breath — just as A He's page had it, word for word: after a metal blade, he needs a breath — and only then did his left hand press down, and before Xiaoman an earth wall heaved up with a boom, chest-high, crowding him toward the edge. In the space of that breath Xiaoman already had both hands ready. His right threw a fire bolt at the wall, which only blackened a patch; his left followed with a flick, and a wood vine burrowed out from the foot of the wall, and the wall cracked — the fire was for Lu Fang to watch; the wood was what eats earth. Someone below said "Eh?" — "Brother Lu needs a breath to switch — he… he threw two kinds in one breath?" For the first time Lu Fang's eyelids lifted.

label.en: Watch his feet; wait for the wind

exits.means: fights Lu Fang of the inner court; hanging from the rim, flings out the first thing in his pouch — the Beef-Tallow Nectar jar — and Lu Fang's stamp slips on it, off the stage

withdrawn.zh: 卢方抖了抖袖子，眼皮又耷拉了下来：「外门的。」——再来。
withdrawn.en: Lu Fang shakes out his sleeves, eyelids drooping again: "Outer court." — Again.

story.zh:
他从那道缝里一掌穿了过来。六层的掌，比何七的拳快了一倍不止。小满看脚，看得见他往哪里去，身子却跟不上：头一掌擦着他的肩膀过去，第二掌他躲开了，第三掌正打在他左肋上，「咔」的一声，秘境里断过的那根骨头，又裂了。他整个人横着飞出去，滚了三滚，滚到了台边，半个身子已经挂在了外头，两只手扒着青石板的边沿，十个指头死死地抠着，底下是演武场的冻土。台下一片惊叫，跟着便有人笑：「完了完了，下去吧！」

卢方走过来，低头看着他扒在石沿上的那两只手，抬起右脚，一脚踩在他左手背上，碾了一碾。跟方才踩孙二狗，一模一样。

那一碾，碾得小满眼前一黑。疼还在其次；他扒在那里，看着那只踩在自己手背上的脚，心里生出来的，是怕。不是怕疼，是怕自己下去。他一下去，孙二狗那七回，就是白倒的。

他的右手松了石沿，往腰上的储物袋里乱摸——左手叫那只脚钉在石头上，倒成了他身上唯一挂得住的地方。摸着什么是什么，他没工夫看，一把掏出来，往石沿上一砸，右手又扒了回去。

「啪」的一声，一只小陶罐碎在青石板上，红油溅开一片，花椒粒子滚了一地。牛脂甘露。台下前排的人一齐吸了吸鼻子。

卢方低头看了一眼，冷笑道：「这是什么？」他的重心全压在左脚跟上，右脚从小满手背上抬了起来，抬得比头一下还高——要跺。小满不看那只抬起来的脚，看它要落的地方：自己那只左手，和左手边那一摊红油。他爹在黑松岭的山涧边上讲过：天下的鹿，都是先动脚。风从北边山口灌过来，扑在卢方背上，吹得他袍子往前一鼓。先看风，后看鹿。

卢方的右脚跺下来了。小满把左手往旁边一抽。

那一脚没跺着手，跺在了牛油上。六层的一脚，使足了劲，收不住，鞋底在油上「哧」地一溜，溜出了台沿，人只剩左脚跟还挨着石头。小满抽回来的那只左手，五个指头不听使唤，拿手腕在那只脚踝上一勾，背后那一阵风再一推——卢方整个人从小满头顶上翻了过去，「砰」的一声，脸朝下摔在台下的冻土上。

小满一只手挂在石沿上，晃了两晃，自己爬了上来，跪在台边，喘。满台的花椒味。

演武场上静了。静了足有一口气的工夫，才有一个声音道：「……外门的？」又一个声音：「四层？把内门的六层……扔下去了？」人堆里「轰」的一声，炸了。石阶上，孙二狗一下子站了起来，忘了自己那只手，拿那只缠着布的肿手往天上一举，扯着嗓子喊：「沈师兄——！」喊破了音。

执事张了两回嘴，才道：「……沈小满，胜。」

台下，卢方趴在冻土上，半天没有起来。他撑起半个身子，低头看着自己那只右脚——熬了九年才熬进内门的那只脚，鞋底上一层红油——看了一会儿，一拳砸在冻土上。小满跪在台边看着他。他以为自己会痛快的。那一脚滑出去的时候，是痛快的；这时候，他只觉得肋下一阵一阵地抽，左手背上一个青紫的鞋印，心里空了一块，像一口缸，水倒干净了，只剩一个缸底。他爬起来，走下了台，没有回头。

他走到石阶跟前，在孙二狗旁边坐下，背过身去，从腰上的储物袋里摸出那只小瓷瓶。三颗回春丹，一颗方才进了孙二狗的肚子；他倒出第二颗，吞了。一道暖从肚里爬上来，那根裂了的骨头先是一烫，跟着一麻；左手背上那个鞋印，青紫褪成了黄。一道纹的丹，接得上骨头，接不全；他按了按肋下，还疼，疼得喘得上气了。五个指头攥了攥，攥得拢。

老槐树底下，钱掌柜把「一百」抹了，写上「二十」。有人跺脚：「我上一场押的是一百！」钱掌柜拨着算盘：「押出去的，照押出去的算。」
story.en:
He drove a palm through the crack. A layer-six palm was more than twice as fast as He Qi's fist. Xiaoman watched the feet and could see where it was going, but his body couldn't keep up: the first palm grazed his shoulder, the second he dodged, the third landed square on his left ribs — crack — and the bone broken in the hidden realm split again. He flew sideways, rolled three times, rolled to the edge, half his body already hanging over, both hands clawing the rim of the bluestone, ten fingers dug in, the frozen earth of the training ground below. Screams below, and then laughter: "That's it, that's it, get down!"

Lu Fang walked over, looked down at the two hands clinging to the stone rim, lifted his right foot, and stamped on the back of Xiaoman's left hand, and ground it. Exactly as he had stamped on Sun Ergou.

That grinding turned Xiaoman's sight black. The pain was the least of it; clinging there, looking at the foot on his hand, what rose in him was fear. Not of pain; of going down. If he went down, Sun Ergou's seven falls were for nothing.

His right hand let go of the rim and groped in the storage pouch at his waist — the left, nailed to the stone under that foot, had become the one thing holding him on. Whatever his hand found, it found; he had no time to look. He pulled it out, smashed it down on the rim, and clawed the stone again.

*Crack* — a little clay jar broke on the bluestone; red oil splashed wide and peppercorns rolled everywhere. Beef-Tallow Nectar. The front row all sniffed at once.

Lu Fang glanced down and sneered: "What's this?" All his weight was on his left heel; his right foot came up off Xiaoman's hand, higher than the first time — to stamp. Xiaoman didn't watch the raised foot; he watched where it would land: his own left hand, and the slick of red oil beside it. By the stream at Black Pine Ridge his father had told him: every deer under heaven moves its feet first. Wind poured in from the northern pass and struck Lu Fang's back, puffing his robe forward. Watch the wind first, then the deer.

Lu Fang's right foot came down. Xiaoman snatched his left hand aside.

The stamp found no hand; it found tallow. A layer six's stamp, all his strength behind it, couldn't be stopped: the sole went *hiss* across the oil and shot off the rim, and he was left with only his left heel on the stone. Xiaoman's snatched-back left hand — the fingers wouldn't obey — hooked that ankle with the wrist, the wind at the man's back gave one more push — and Lu Fang went clean over Xiaoman's head and hit the frozen earth below face-first — thud.

Xiaoman hung by one hand from the rim, swung twice, climbed back up by himself, and knelt at the edge, panting. The whole stage smelled of Sichuan pepper.

The training ground went silent. A full breath of silence before one voice said: "…Outer court?" And another: "Layer four? Threw an inner layer six… off the stage?" The crowd exploded. On the steps Sun Ergou shot to his feet, forgot his hand, flung the swollen bandaged thing up at the sky, and bawled: "Brother Shen —!" — his voice cracking.

The steward opened his mouth twice before he said: "…Shen Xiaoman wins."

Below, Lu Fang lay on the frozen earth a long while without rising. He pushed up on one arm and looked at his own right foot — the foot that had taken nine years to grind its way into the inner court, its sole slick with red oil — looked a while, then drove a fist into the frozen ground. Xiaoman knelt at the edge and watched him. He had thought it would feel good. In the moment the foot went, it had; now there was only the pulling in his ribs, a purple footprint on the back of his left hand, and a hollow in his chest, like a vat with the water poured out and only the bottom left. He got up and walked down off the stage and didn't look back.

He went to the stone steps, sat down beside Sun Ergou, turned his back, and took the little porcelain bottle from the storage pouch at his waist. Three Spring-Return pills: one had just gone into Sun Ergou; he shook out the second and swallowed it. Warmth climbed up from his belly; the cracked bone burned first, then went numb, and the footprint on the back of his left hand faded from purple to yellow. A one-line pill could set a bone, not make it whole; he pressed his ribs — still sore, but sore enough to breathe through now. He closed his five fingers: they closed.

Under the pagoda tree Money-Keeper Qian rubbed out "a hundred" and wrote "twenty." Someone stamped: "I put mine down at a hundred last round!" Clicking his abacus: "What went out at a price is reckoned at that price."
